result:
The proposed answer is wrong, and its stated final line is also garbled.

Alice is the robber and Bob is the cop, and Alice can evade forever exactly when the graph is not cop-win, meaning it is not dismantlable.

**Upper bound.** If any vertex is adjacent to all others, Bob starts there and wins. So every vertex needs at least one non-neighbor. The complement graph then has minimum degree at least 1, so it has at least n edges (a perfect matching is the cheapest way to achieve that). The original graph therefore has at most C(2n,2) − n = 2n² − n − n = 2n(n−1) edges.

**Achievability.** Take K_{2n} minus a perfect matching, the cocktail-party graph. For two distinct vertices u and v, the closed neighborhood N[v] is everything except v′, the partner of v. The partner u′ of u lies in N[v] unless u′ = v, but u′ is not in N[u]. So N[v] ⊄ N[u], which means no vertex is dominated and the graph is not dismantlable. Hence Alice evades Bob indefinitely.

Check: n = 2 gives C₄ with 4 edges. n = 3 gives the octahedron with 12 edges.

The correct maximum is 2n(n−1) for every n > 1. The proposed solution gives n² for n = 3 (that is, 9), where the true value is 12. It also gives 2n² − 2n − 1 for odd n ≥ 5, which is one less than the true value.

VERDICT: REJECT
